problem:
Meridian Bank is migrating customer data from a legacy core system to a new platform. During the first rehearsal, the migration report shows thousands of mismatches: names that do not match, addresses that cannot be placed into the new structured format, dates in different formats, and payment records whose beneficiary details are incomplete. The programme manager must decide whether the migration is safe to proceed, and the business analyst must define the mapping, the transformation rules, the control totals and the exception handling before the next rehearsal.

The risk is that the new platform goes live with wrong customer data, so payments fail validation, statements go to the wrong address, and screening misses a match. The risk in the other direction is that the team invents data to fill the gaps, for example by guessing address components or payment values that the legacy record never held. The migration must be proven correct before sign-off, not fixed after go-live.
solution:
Define the migration as a controlled data movement with proof at every stage. Start with a field-level mapping from the legacy system to the new platform: every source field, its target field, its transformation rule, its validation rule and its owner. Where the target needs a value the source does not hold, do not fabricate it. Identify whether the value can be derived from trusted contextual data, such as a settlement arrangement or a correspondent relationship, document the derivation rule and its confidence, and hold the record for repair where no valid derivation exists.

Handle addresses with particular care. The requirement is a structured or hybrid address with at least a town name and country code, or a BIC only where that is permitted, and the timeline for structured addresses has been extended, so no fixed cut-off date should be taught or used as a project deadline. Legacy free-text addresses that cannot be safely decomposed must follow an approved remediation or exception process, with customer outreach where the address is needed for payments. Never split a free-text address into structured components by guessing.

Run control totals at each stage: record counts, total balances, and counts by customer type, so a lost or duplicated record is visible immediately. Classify exceptions by cause, age them, and assign owners. Run the migration in rehearsal, compare the new platform against the legacy system record by record for a sample and in full for control totals, and only sign off when the residual exceptions are listed, understood and owned, with a plan and a date for each. Keep the original legacy record for audit, and make the migration reversible until the new platform is proven in production.

decision.question: During a migration rehearsal, thousands of customer records mismatch between the legacy system and the new platform, including addresses that cannot be placed into the new structured format. What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.detail: Proceed to go-live and fix mismatches afterwards.

options.label: B
options.detail: Stop, define the field mapping and transformation rules, run control totals, classify exceptions, fix the source data or the mapping, and require sign-off only when the residuals are understood and owned.

options.label: C
options.detail: Migrate only the records that match and leave the rest behind without a record.

options.label: D
options.detail: Guess the missing address components so the records pass validation.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because migration quality must be proven before go-live, and every exception needs a known cause, an owner and a planned treatment. Option A puts wrong data into production. Option D invents data the source never held. Option C loses customer records silently.

steps.title: Defines the field-level mapping, transformation rules and validation rules
Extracts customer data from the legacy system with control totals
Transforms the data to the new platform format, applying documented derivation rules only
Validates each record against the new platform rules and routes failures to exceptions
Reviews exceptions, fixes source data or the mapping, and requests missing data from customers where needed
Loads the validated records into the new platform
Reconciles record counts, balances and control totals between legacy and new systems
Signs off only when residuals are listed, understood and owned, with a plan for each

happy: The mapping is agreed, transformation rules are documented, and the rehearsal loads cleanly. Control totals match between the legacy system and the new platform, exceptions are few and each has an owner and a plan, structured addresses validate correctly, and sign-off is given with a short, named residual list. Go-live proceeds with the legacy record retained for audit.

negative.title: Mandatory target value missing from source
negative.detail: A legacy MT message or customer record lacks a value the new ISO 20022 message requires. Do not fabricate the value. Derive it only from trusted contextual data under a documented rule, or hold the payment or record for repair.

negative.title: Structured address cannot be derived
negative.detail: A legacy free-text address cannot be safely split into structured components. Follow the approved remediation or exception process, seek the correct address from the customer where needed, and do not guess components.

negative.title: Incomplete beneficiary data
negative.detail: A migrated payment record omits a beneficiary address required for a destination. Validate requirements by rail and destination, use trusted beneficiary data only where policy permits, and request correction before submission.

negative.title: Control totals do not match
negative.detail: Record counts or balances differ between the legacy system and the new platform. Stop the load, find the stage where the totals diverged, and fix the mapping or the extraction before proceeding.

technical: Maintain a source-to-target mapping with derivation rules, confidence levels, data provenance and negative tests. Keep the original legacy message and record for audit, and record the transformation applied to every field. Use control totals at extraction, transformation, validation and load, and reconcile them at each stage. Validate addresses against the structured or hybrid requirement, with town name and country code as the minimum, and never invent components. Handle character sets explicitly: apply documented transliteration only where permitted, preserve the original customer-provided value, and record the transformed value. Version the mapping, test it with representative and edge-case records, and make the migration reversible until production is proven.

messages.title: Customer payment message in the new ISO 20022 format, produced from the legacy record.

fields.tag: Structured or hybrid postal address, town name and country code as minimum
fields.name: Structured or hybrid postal address, town name and country code as minimum

messages.title: Financial institution to financial institution payment, used for the cover or settlement leg where applicable.
Legacy MT103 customer payment mapped to the ISO 20022 customer payment.
Legacy MT202 COV cover payment mapped to the ISO 20022 financial institution payment.

accounting: Customer balances and payment records must reconcile between the legacy system and the new platform to the cent, with control totals for record counts and total balances. No balance may be adjusted to make totals match; a difference is an exception to be investigated. Migrated payment records that cannot be validated must not be submitted to clearing. Exceptions sit on a worklist with an owner, an age and a service level, and aged items escalate before go-live. The migration sign-off records the residual exceptions, their owners and their planned resolution dates, and the legacy system is retained until the new platform is proven in production.

scenarios.given: a mandatory target field cannot be reliably derived
scenarios.then: the payment is held for repair rather than populated with an invented value.

scenarios.given: a legacy unstructured address cannot be safely decomposed
scenarios.then: the payment follows the approved remediation or exception process.

scenarios.given: a destination requires a beneficiary address
scenarios.then: the API returns a specific validation error and does not create a payment.

questions.question: A target ISO 20022 field has no value in the legacy source. What should happen?
options: Derive it only from trusted contextual data under a documented rule, or hold the record for repair.
Leave the field blank and send the payment.
Copy a value from another record.
questions.explanation: A mandatory value must never be fabricated. It is derived only where a documented rule allows it, or the record is held.

questions.question: What is the minimum for a structured or hybrid address?
options: Town name and country code, or a BIC only where permitted.
questions.explanation: The requirement is a structured or hybrid address with at least town name and country code, or a BIC only where that is permitted.

questions.question: How is migration quality proven before sign-off?
options: By the number of records loaded.
By control totals at each stage, record-by-record comparison, and a listed, owned residual exception list.
questions.explanation: Control totals, comparison and a named residual list prove the migration. Volume alone proves nothing.

questions.question: A legacy free-text address cannot be safely split into structured parts. What is correct?
options: Split it by guessing the town and street.
Follow the approved remediation or exception process and seek the correct address where needed.
questions.explanation: Guessing address components invents data. The approved remediation process protects the customer and the payment.
